title: Everything from one break now sinks together
question: Does the descent read right now — one group going down at one pace, rather than some of it arriving while the rest is still at the surface?
context_md:
*"Much better. But it falls at slightly odd rates. There is a first group of chunks that drop too fast and then the rest that come together with the grit later."*

Reproduced exactly, and the cause turned out to be that **nothing had ever slowed a body down in water.** A piece kept the speed it built up in the air and went on building more all the way to the bottom.

| | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| fastest a piece ever went | **6.00 cells a frame** — the engine's own speed cap | 2.58, and that is the moment of entry |
| its speed over the descent | 0.14 to 6.00, all over the place | a steady ~1.8 |
| what is left of the slab | 422 of 600 cells still stone | 421 |

The surprise is *where* the 6.00 happens: twenty rows of falling through air only gets a piece to 1.4. The other thirty rows of acceleration are **underwater**. That is your first group — pieces that went in fast and kept going.

Water pushes back now, in two ways: **buoyancy**, so a piece only feels the weight it has over the water it displaces (heavy rock sinks faster than light, and something barely denser than water barely sinks at all), and a **terminal speed** it cannot exceed.

**A speed limit rather than a drag, and I tried it the other way first.** Proper drag is the nicer model and gives the same even descent — and it costs rock, because it slows the *whole* fall rather than only its fast end, so pieces arrive later and one at a time onto a pile that is already there, and get broken up again. Drag leaves **341 of 600 cells as stone**; the speed limit leaves **420**; doing nothing leaves 450 and shows the fault. The limit buys the look for almost nothing.

**It is worth more on lava than on rock.** The quenched crust in a lava pour goes from **91 cells of surviving stone to 378** — four times as much — which is the other half of what you said about chunks turning to dust.

Both clips are the same drop at true speed.

items.label: before
items.caption: Pieces on the floor while others are still at the surface. Fastest: 6.00 cells a frame.

items.label: now
items.caption: One group, one pace. Fastest: 2.58, at the moment of entry.
